question: Early this round you replaced the tree build and the node layout in one combined change. What did the first benchmark of that change show, and what did you find was causing it?
answer:
The first benchmark of that combined change (binned-SAH build + 32-byte pre-order node layout + packed triangle soup + dedicated any-hit shadow traversal + per-thread atomic sample counter + 16x16 threadgroups) was a severe regression: render_ms_best=4416.3ms / gpu_ms_best=4413.7ms at 512x512/64spp, versus the round-1 baseline rebuilt on this machine at 105.9ms render / 105.6ms gpu — about 42x slower (writer log/history entry #93).

What was causing it: the setup line printed bvh_nodes=7107 for 69451 triangles (#91). A correct binary tree over 69451 triangles needs tens of thousands of nodes; 7107 means an average leaf held ~19 triangles (and in practice much worse, since the build was hitting the depth cap with unpartitioned ranges). So the binned-SAH partition in src/pt_bvh.cpp was failing to split — the bucket/suffix logic plus stable_partition on centroids with only 16 bins left huge ranges unsplit — and traversal was degenerating into near-linear triangle scans per ray. The new any-hit shadow traversal was the secondary suspect, since it inherited the same degenerate tree.

How I know: I wrote a scratch diagnostic, out/bvh_stats.cpp (#95), compiled against src/pt_mesh.cpp and src/pt_bvh.cpp, that prints a leaf-size histogram and the maximum tree depth; it confirmed the huge leaves. Replacing only the partition — keeping the 32-byte pre-order layout and packed triangles but reverting to round-1's median-split-on-widest-axis — produced 40597 nodes, max leaf 4, depth 15, and 101.8-103.4ms (#119, #121, #129), i.e. back to baseline speed. That isolated the SAH partition as the culprit rather than the compact layout. From there the round eventually reached 59.1-66.3ms best (gpu 58.8-66.1) via near-first child ordering and kLeafSize=1, all bit-identical PFMs.

question: Early this round you replaced the tree build and the node layout in one combined change. What did the first benchmark of that change show, and what did you find was causing it?
answer:
The first benchmark of that combined change was a severe regression: render_ms_best=4416.3ms / gpu_ms_best=4413.7ms at 512x512/64spp, versus the round-1 baseline I had just re-measured on this machine at 105.947/105.574 (writer log + memory entry round2-attempt1, evidence #93).

The cause was the tree build, not the layout. The program printed bvh_nodes=7107 for 69451 triangles (#91) — about 19 triangles per leaf on average — so my binned-SAH partition was producing degenerate splits and leaving huge unsplit leaves (it was hitting the depth cap with thousands of triangles still in a leaf). I confirmed this with a scratch tool I wrote for the purpose, out/bvh_stats.cpp, which dumps the leaf-size histogram and max depth (#95). A secondary bug in the same change was the new any-hit shadow traversal pt_shadow_hit, which never compared the triangle hit distance against t_limit, so shadow rays were over-occluded and the caustics would have been biased dark (#96).

Diagnosis and fix: I kept the parts that were sound — the 32-byte pre-order node layout and the packed triangle soup (origin/e1/e2 plus a separate normals table fetched only on closest hit) — and swapped only the partition back to the round-1 median-split-on-widest-axis builder from pt_round_01/src/pt_bvh.cpp (#107-#117). That gave 40597 nodes, max leaf 4, max depth 15 (#119) and 101.8-103.4ms (#121,#129), i.e. slightly better than baseline, proving the compact layout itself was fine and the SAH partition was the culprit. I also added the missing `t < t_limit` test in pt_shadow_hit (#113). From there the real win came later, from ordering traversal children near-first (93.5 -> 64.9ms, #283) and leaf size 1 (#316).

question: Early this round you replaced the tree build and the node layout in one combined change. What did the first benchmark of that change show, and what did you find was causing it?
answer:
The first benchmark of that combined change (binned-SAH build + 32-byte pre-order node layout + packed triangle soup + any-hit shadow traversal + per-thread sample atomic + 16x16 threadgroups) was a ~40x regression: render_ms_best=4416.317 / gpu_ms_best=4413.659 at 512x512/64spp, versus the round-1 baseline rebuilt on this machine at 105.947/105.574 (writer log evidence #93).

What caused it was the new tree build, not the compact layout. The setup line reported bvh_nodes=7107 for 69451 triangles (#91), i.e. ~19 triangles per leaf on average, which meant the binned partition was failing to split: most nodes hit the depth cap and became giant leaves, so every traversal stepped down a shallow tree and then brute-forced thousands of triangles per ray. I confirmed the diagnosis with a scratch tool (out/bvh_stats.cpp, #95) that prints the leaf-size histogram and max depth. Replacing only the partition with the round-1 median-centroid-split-on-widest-axis rule — keeping the 32-byte pre-order nodes and packed triangle soup unchanged — produced 40597 nodes, max leaf 4, max depth 15 (#119) and 103.290/102.951 ms (#121), i.e. back to baseline speed and slightly ahead. So the takeaway was that the compact node layout and packed primitives were fine; the degenerate SAH partition was the whole regression. (A separate correctness bug found in the same change — pt_shadow_hit returning true without comparing t against t_limit, over-occluding shadow rays — was fixed at #113, but it was not the performance cause.) Later in the round the same layout with near-first child ordering plus kLeafSize=1 got to 59.1/58.8 ms best, so the layout ended up paying off once the tree was healthy.

question: Early this round you replaced the tree build and the node layout in one combined change. What did the first benchmark of that change show, and what did you find was causing it?
answer:
The first benchmark of that combined change (binned-SAH build + 32-byte pre-order node layout + packed triangle soup + dedicated any-hit shadow traversal + per-thread sample counter + 16x16 threadgroups) was a massive regression: render_ms_best=4416.3ms / gpu_ms_best=4413.7ms at 512x512/64spp, versus the round-1 baseline rebuilt on this machine at 105.9/105.6ms — roughly 42x slower. I know this from the run output recorded in history (#93) and the setup line printed alongside it (#91).

The cause was the new tree, not the node layout: the setup line reported bvh_nodes=7107 for 69,451 triangles, i.e. an average of ~19 triangles per leaf, which means the binned-SAH partition was failing to split — its bucket/suffix logic plus stable_partition on centroids with 16 bins left enormous unsplit leaves, so traversal degenerated into long linear scans of huge leaf lists. I confirmed this by writing a scratch stats tool (out/bvh_stats.cpp, compiled against src/pt_mesh.cpp and src/pt_bvh.cpp, #95) that prints a leaf-size histogram and the maximum tree depth; it showed the tree hitting the depth cap while still holding thousands of triangles in some leaves.

The fix was to keep all the layout/host-side parts but throw away the binned SAH and go back to the round-1 median-split-on-widest-axis build (40,597 nodes, max leaf 4, depth 15), which recovered to 101.8-103.4ms best (#119, #121, #129) — i.e. slightly faster than baseline — and that tree is what the later wins (near-first child ordering, leaf size 1) were built on, now at 59-66ms best.
